text: Your mettle is your ability to hold up and perform when things get hard: nerve, grit and staying power under pressure, rather than raw talent. It almost always appears in the phrase test someone's mettle, and though it sounds like metal and once meant the quality of a blade's steel, today it is only ever used about people. Saying the best teenage mathematicians tested their mettle at the Olympiads means they sat down against the strongest competition on earth, on a clock, and held up.

A vestige is the small surviving trace of something that used to be far bigger, the bit left over once the rest is gone. Biologists use it for body parts whose job disappeared long ago, such as a whale's hip bones, and writers use it for habits and institutions that are nearly extinct. Here the loud, physically imposing Wall Street trader has almost vanished from finance, so corporate-bond trading is called perhaps his last vestige, the final corner where that old type still survives.

Commensurate means matching in size or degree, so that one thing is as large as the other deserves. It nearly always arrives with with: pay commensurate with experience, a punishment commensurate with the crime. The closing line argues that Olympiad Man's brilliance is now enormous while his demonstrated virtue has not grown to match it, and that until it does he is better off staying poorly understood.

To comprise something is to be made up of it, to consist of its parts. Careful writers use it in the direction shown here, where the whole comes first and the parts follow: society comprises men of gold, silver and bronze. It is a more formal cousin of consists of, and you will meet it constantly in descriptions of committees, alloys and populations.

Relentless describes something that never lets up, never pauses and never softens, from a root meaning to slacken. It carries a hint of being wearing or unstoppable rather than merely fast. Calling the advances in AI relentless suggests they arrive one after another with no breathing space, which is why the researchers described here gave up and resigned.

A squad is the full group of people selected to represent a team, from which the ones who actually play are then chosen. It comes from the military, where a squad is the smallest unit of soldiers. Saying Dario Amodei was a member of the squad but not quite the starting line-up of America's physics side means he made the team but was not among those picked to compete.

A company's board, short for board of directors, is the small group elected to oversee the people who run it day to day, with the power to approve big decisions and to fire the chief executive. This is a completely separate sense from a plank of wood or a board game. Appointing Paul Christiano to the board puts an AI-safety specialist at the level that supervises OpenAI's bosses rather than merely working for them.

To ace something is to do it perfectly or score top marks on it, from the ace that is the highest card and, in tennis, an unreturnable serve. It is informal but extremely common in American English about tests and interviews. Saying Olympiad Man was acing maths competitions before his first drink emphasises how young he was when he began winning outright.

To decamp is to leave somewhere suddenly and go elsewhere, originally a military word meaning to break camp and move on. It often carries a faint suggestion of abandoning the place you were. Noam Shazeer decamped to OpenAI, meaning Google paid an enormous sum to hire him and he then left for a rival.

To moonlight is to hold a second job alongside your main one, named for the idea of working after dark. It usually implies the side job is unusual, unofficial or done for love rather than money. OpenAI's head researcher has moonlighted as head coach of America's informatics team, running the national squad on top of a demanding day job.

An archetype is the original model that later examples copy, so archetypal means being the purest, most typical example of a type. It sits somewhere between typical and definitive. Calling Sheryl Sandberg the archetypal Davos Woman says she was not merely one example of the globe-trotting corporate executive but the clearest one.

To best someone is to beat or outdo them in a contest, a verb made from the adjective best. It sounds slightly old-fashioned or literary compared with beat, and suits a fight or a rivalry. Jane Street is besting banks in corporate-bond trading, that is, winning business away from firms that used to dominate it.

A jock is American slang for a sporty, physically imposing person, often with the implied jab that brawn matters more to them than brains. It is the traditional opposite of a nerd. The Wall Street jock is the old type of trader who succeeded by being loud, quick and aggressive on a crowded floor, and the article says mathematicians have replaced him.

To dabble in something is to do a little of it casually, without committing fully, from the image of splashing your hand in shallow water. It can be neutral or gently dismissive. Saying Jane Street dabbles in venture capital means backing startups is a sideline for the firm rather than its main business.

Literally, illiterate means unable to read and write, but it is used far more often to mean ignorant or unschooled about something. Paired here with numerate, it sets up a contrast between crooks who know nothing and specialists who know mathematics. Describing cryptocurrency as full of illiterate spivs but also numerate swots says the field attracts both kinds at once.

Numerate means comfortable and skilled with numbers, the mathematical counterpart of literate. It is far more common in British than American English, and job adverts there often ask for numerate graduates. It marks the second half of the contrast in cryptocurrency, between people who understand nothing and people who understand the maths.

A spiv is British slang for a flashy small-time crook who lives by shady deals rather than honest work, a word from 1940s black-market London. It suggests showiness and dishonesty together. Calling part of the cryptocurrency world illiterate spivs is a blunt way of saying it is full of chancers selling things they do not understand.

A swot is British slang for someone who studies extremely hard, roughly what Americans call a grind or, less kindly, a nerd; to swot is to study intensively. It can be mocking or admiring depending on the speaker. Here the numerate swots are the mathematically serious people in cryptocurrency, set against the spivs.

A namesake is a person or thing that shares a name with another, in either direction: you can be someone's namesake or they can be yours. It is a plain word for a relationship that otherwise takes a whole clause to express. The Olympiads' sporting namesakes are the Olympic Games, from which the competitions borrowed both the name and the gold, silver and bronze medals.

To rear a child or an animal is to raise it to adulthood, caring for it and bringing it up. This is a different verb from the one that describes a horse rearing up on its hind legs. The business of rearing and attracting Olympiad Men means growing this kind of talent at home through schools and training, as opposed to importing it from abroad.

Slick describes something smooth, polished and practised, and about a person it is almost always a criticism: too smooth to be quite trusted. Its literal sense is slippery, as in an oil slick. The slick corporate executive is the Davos type whose polish is exactly what makes ordinary people suspicious of him.

To audit something is to check it carefully against the evidence, most familiarly a company's accounts, from a Latin root meaning to hear. It has spread well beyond finance: you can audit a data set, an algorithm or a claim. The ability to audit one's power means anyone can check how Olympiad Man got his position, because a medal from a public competition is a verifiable record.

To hold something in contempt is to regard it as worthless and beneath you, so contemptuous means openly scornful. It is stronger and colder than critical or disapproving. Saying societies are both contemptuous and envious of elites captures the doubleness of the feeling: people look down on the powerful and want to be them at the same time.

As a noun, a corrective is something that fixes an error or counteracts a bias, not the act of punishing someone. You offer a corrective to a mistaken view the way a weight balances a scale. Studying Olympiad Man is called a corrective to bad views on immigration because the facts about where this talent comes from cut against what both political sides assume.

In a university, the faculty is the teaching staff taken as a group, and in American usage it usually means all the professors at an institution. The same word separately means a natural ability, as in the faculty of speech, and in Britain a division of a university. Buckley preferred being governed by names from a telephone directory over the faculty at Harvard, meaning ordinary people over credentialed academics.

A register here is an official written list of people or things, such as a register of voters or of births. This is separate from the verb to register, or from register meaning a level of formality in speech. A register of Olympiad Men would be the roll of everyone who has won a medal, imagined as a pool from which rulers might be drawn.

To be abstracted from something is to be drawn away and separated from it, a stronger and more physical sense than the everyday abstract meaning theoretical. Someone abstracted is detached, removed, not in contact. Saying Olympiad Man is truly abstracted from the world argues he is cut off from ordinary life in a way even other elites are not.

In philosophy a rationalist holds that reason, rather than experience, is the main route to knowledge. The word also names a modern online subculture, strongly represented in AI labs, that tries to reason about beliefs using probabilities and formal arguments and is closely tied to effective altruism. It is that second sense in play when the article says his rationalist philosophy would strike ordinary folk as a mark of insanity.

Unintelligible means impossible to understand, built from intelligible, meaning able to be grasped. It is usually said of speech, handwriting or reasoning. The twist here is the reason given: Olympiad Man's language is unintelligible not because it is complicated but because nobody believes what he is saying.

To speak glibly is to speak fluently and easily about something that deserves more care, so the ease itself becomes the criticism. A glib answer is smooth, quick and shallow. Saying AI researchers talk glibly about p doom means they discuss the chance their technology destroys the world in the casual tone other people use for the weather.

The populace is the general body of ordinary people in a country, the population considered as the public. It is a formal word and often carries a faint distance, as if viewed from above. Saying the populace is yet to fully comprehend Olympiad Man means the wider public has not yet grasped who these people are or how much power they hold.

Globalisation is the process by which trade, money, ideas and people move more freely across national borders, knitting countries into one economy. The spelling with an s is British; American writing uses globalization. Olympiad Man's vision of globalisation is talent moving across borders, a Romanian or Indian teenager ending up in an American lab, rather than the executive-and-conference version associated with Davos.

To cut your teeth on something is to get your first real experience and training there, borrowed from babies growing their first teeth. The place named is where you learned the trade. Davos Man cut his teeth at McKinsey in his 20s, meaning the consulting firm is where that kind of executive was formed.

The ranks of a group means its membership, the body of people in it, from the rows soldiers stand in on parade. You rise through the ranks, join the ranks, or emerge from the ranks. Saying an elite has emerged from the ranks of the winners means it was drawn out of the whole population of medallists.

In team sports the starting line-up is the group actually sent out to begin the game, as opposed to the wider squad of substitutes and reserves. Making the squad and making the starting line-up are two different achievements. Dario Amodei was on America's physics side but not quite the starting line-up, a sporting way of saying he was very good but not one of the very best.

When one thing gives way to another it yields its place and is replaced by it, the way a wooden floor gives way underfoot. It is the standard phrase for one era or fashion succeeding another. The broad shoulders of pit trading gave way to the narrow ones that build algorithms, meaning the physical trader was replaced by the programmer.

God knows is an everyday exclamation meaning nobody has any idea, with no religious content intended. It is a shrug in words, usually answering a question the speaker thinks is unanswerable. Asked how one becomes a Young Global Leader at the World Economic Forum, the answer God knows is a jab at how opaque the selection is.

To be a class apart is to belong to a separate and usually superior category, set off from everyone else. Class here means a group or rank of people rather than a lesson. Saying elites are by necessity a class apart from their subjects means separation is built into what being an elite is.

Tacked onto a negative, to speak of means worth mentioning, so few friends to speak of means hardly any at all. It is a quiet way of turning a small number into effectively none. He has few employees to speak of underlines how small these enormously valuable firms are.

Plato was an Athenian philosopher of the fourth century BC and a founding figure of Western thought. In his book the Republic he imagines an ideal city sorted into three groups by a founding myth: people of gold who rule, of silver who are soldiers, and of bronze who farm. The article opens there because the Olympiads hand out gold, silver and bronze too, and then asks whether their winners really are fit to rule.

An Olympiad here is an international academic competition for school students, not a sporting event. The International Mathematical Olympiad began in 1959 in communist Romania; each country sends a small team, competitors sit several hours of extremely hard problems over two days, and gold, silver and bronze medals are awarded. Parallel Olympiads now run in physics, chemistry, biology and informatics.

Informatics is the study of information and computation, essentially what Americans call computer science. The word is standard in Europe, which is why the competition is the International Olympiad in Informatics. The article glosses it as computing for exactly that reason.

A problem set is a batch of hard problems assigned to be worked through, the standard homework format in university maths, physics and computer science. Competitive students spend years on them. Saying Alexandr Wang is not long off America's problem-set circuit means he was recently one of the teenagers travelling to these competitions.

Anthropic is an American artificial-intelligence company, founded in 2021 by former OpenAI staff, that builds large AI models and puts unusual public emphasis on making them safe. It is one of a handful of labs at the frontier of the technology. The article uses it as its first example because two of its researchers resigned over how fast the models were improving.

Dario Amodei is the co-founder and chief executive of Anthropic and a physicist by training, previously a research lead at OpenAI. He is known for arguing publicly that AI is both extraordinarily valuable and genuinely dangerous. He appears here as an Olympiad Man himself, having been on America's physics squad.

AI safety is the field concerned with making sure powerful artificial-intelligence systems do what people actually want and cannot cause catastrophic harm. It covers technical work on controlling and testing models as well as arguments about how fast to build them. Paul Christiano, appointed to OpenAI's board, is one of its best-known researchers.

McKinsey and Company is the most famous management-consulting firm in the world: companies and governments pay it to advise them on strategy and reorganisation. For decades it was the standard first job for ambitious graduates heading into corporate leadership. That is why the article says Davos Man cut his teeth there, and the contrast with a maths competition is the point.

Davos Man is a term coined in 2004 by the political scientist Samuel Huntington for the globe-trotting corporate elite who gather each January at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland. It describes someone whose loyalty is to the world economy rather than to any one country: at home in Singapore, London or New York. It is now used mostly as a criticism, and this article argues that this type has been displaced.

The World Economic Forum is a Swiss organisation, based near Geneva, best known for the annual meeting it runs each January in the Alpine town of Davos, where thousands of chief executives, heads of government, bankers and campaigners gather for several days of panels and private deals. Attendance is by invitation and a large fee. Its Young Global Leaders programme selects people it deems promising, by a process the article suggests nobody can explain.

Before screens, trading happened by open outcry in a pit: a stepped octagonal area on an exchange floor where traders stood shouting prices and signalling with their hands. Being loud, tall and fast genuinely helped, which is what the broad shoulders refer to. Nearly all of it has been replaced by computers placing orders electronically.

Two Sigma is a large New York trading firm that makes its money by building statistical models of markets rather than by traditional stock-picking. Firms like it are often called quantitative, or quant, funds. Its name comes from the statistical symbol sigma, which measures how far a result sits from average.

Jane Street is a secretive and extremely profitable New York trading firm that quotes buy and sell prices in markets all day and earns the gap between them. It is famous for hiring mathematically gifted young people and for a distinctive puzzle-heavy interview process. The article calls it one of Olympiad Man's favourite employers.

A bond is a loan cut into tradable pieces: a company borrows money and promises to pay interest and then return the original sum on a fixed date. A corporate bond is one issued by a company rather than a government, and these change hands in a market like shares. Bond trading was long dominated by big banks, which is the business Jane Street is now taking.

Venture capital is money invested in young, unproven companies in exchange for a share of ownership, on the expectation that most will fail and a few will be worth enormous sums. It is what funds the AI startups listed here. A firm that dabbles in venture capital is backing startups alongside its main business.

A hedge fund is an investment firm that manages money for wealthy clients and institutions under far looser rules than an ordinary fund, letting it bet that prices will fall as well as rise. The name comes from hedging, meaning to offset one risk with another. They pay very well, which is part of why they attract the same people as the AI labs.

Effective altruism is a movement that tries to work out, using evidence and arithmetic, how to do the greatest possible amount of good with a given amount of money or effort. Its followers rank charities by lives saved per dollar and argue about long-term risks to humanity, including from AI. It overlaps heavily with the rationalist subculture, which is why the article notes AI labs and hedge funds are full of them.

P doom is jargon among AI researchers for the probability that artificial intelligence causes human extinction, with p standing for probability as it does in statistics. People quote their own number, from a fraction of a percent to well above half. The article's point is not that the phrase is hard to decode but that outsiders hear it and simply do not believe the conversation is serious.

The Soviet bloc was the group of communist states in central and eastern Europe led by the Soviet Union from the late 1940s until 1989. Those countries invested heavily in mathematics and physics education and in competitions to find talented children. The first International Mathematical Olympiad was held in Romania in 1959, which is the irony the article draws out: capitalism's biggest prizes now flow through a communist invention.

William F. Buckley junior was an American writer and broadcaster who founded the magazine National Review in 1955 and became the most prominent voice of post-war American conservatism. His best-known line is the one quoted here: he would rather be governed by the first 2,000 names in the Boston telephone directory than by the Harvard faculty. It is an argument that ordinary judgment beats credentialed expertise.
